title: Later Lower
statement: A leaderboard lists scores in arrival order. For each player, count how many players who arrived after them have a strictly lower score. Return the counts in arrival order.

examples.explanation: After 5: 2 and 1 are lower (2). After 2: only 1 (1). After 6: 1 (1). After 1: none.

hints.content: Comparing each player with everyone after them is quadratic.
Process players from the last to the first, so 'players after me' becomes 'players already processed'.
Then each answer is: how many processed scores are smaller than mine? That is a prefix count over score values.
A Fenwick (binary indexed) tree over the score range supports 'add one at value v' and 'count values below v' in O(log range).
Shift scores to positive indices (value + 10001). Merge sort that counts right-side elements jumping ahead is an equally good alternative.

testCases.explanation: After 5: 2 and 1 are lower (2). After 2: only 1 (1). After 6: 1 (1). After 1: none.
Equal scores are not strictly lower.
Many scores, where checking every later player is too slow.

solutions.title: Compare with every later player
solutions.approach: For each i, loop over j > i and count values[j] < values[i].
solutions.pseudocode: for i: out[i] = count of j > i with v[j] < v[i]
solutions.interviewExplanation: The direct count is correct but quadratic, too slow for large boards.

solutions.title: Right-to-left Fenwick tree
solutions.intuition: Scanning from the right turns the question into a running prefix count over values, which a Fenwick tree answers in logarithmic time.
solutions.approach: Use a Fenwick tree indexed by value + 10001. From the last player to the first: the answer is the prefix sum up to value + 10000 (strictly lower), then add one at value + 10001.
solutions.pseudocode: for k from n-1 down to 0: out[k] = prefix(v[k] + offset - 1); add(v[k] + offset)
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log R) for value range R
commonMistakes: Querying the prefix including the value itself, which counts equal scores.
Using a 0-based Fenwick index, where i & -i never advances from 0.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Processing from the right means every inserted score belongs to a later player, so each answer is the number of inserted scores strictly below mine. A Fenwick tree over the shifted score range does each insert and prefix query in O(log R). With a huge value range I'd coordinate-compress first. The merge-sort approach counts, for each left-half element, how many right-half elements were merged before it, and runs in O(n log n).

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: From the right: 1 → query 0, insert 1. 6 → one smaller (1), insert.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: 2 → one smaller (1), insert. 5 → two smaller (1, 2). Output [2, 1, 1, 0].
